title: Spousal IRA Rules and 2026 Contribution Limits
metaDescription: Learn how spousal IRA rules work in 2026, including contribution limits, joint return rules, and traditional or Roth account options.
h1: Spousal IRA Rules and Contribution Limits
cardBlurb: How a non-earning spouse can fund an IRA using joint taxable compensation, with 2026 contribution limits and deduction rules.
introText:
If you file a joint return, you may be able to contribute to an IRA even if you had little or no taxable compensation, as long as your spouse did. A spousal IRA is not a separate account category. It is an [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits) rule that permits an individual with low or zero earnings to make an IRA contribution based on the taxable compensation reported on a joint return.

At ModernWallet, we keep the numbers on this page tied to the IRS pages linked below. Contributions depend on filing status, taxable compensation, and the annual limit.

sections.heading: What a Spousal IRA Is
sections.body:
A spousal IRA is an IRS provision rather than an account product. Under this rule, a spouse with little or no taxable compensation may be able to contribute to a traditional or Roth IRA if the couple files a joint return.

The rule draws on the Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA Limit described in [IRS Publication 590-A](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a). It is a contribution rule, not a separate account type.

sections.heading: The Joint Return and Compensation Rule
sections.body:
If you file a joint return, you may be able to contribute to an IRA even if you did not have taxable compensation, as long as your spouse did. Each spouse can make a contribution up to the current limit.

The total of your combined contributions cannot be more than the taxable compensation reported on your joint return. For example, a hypothetical couple with $12,000 in combined taxable compensation cannot contribute more than $12,000 in combined contributions for that tax year. If combined taxable compensation is less than the annual dollar limit, contributions stop at that lower compensation figure.

sections.heading: The 2026 Contribution Limit
sections.body:
For 2026, total contributions you make each year to all of your traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs cannot exceed $7,500, or $8,600 if you are age 50 or older. If your taxable compensation is less than that amount, the limit is that compensation figure.

Because each spouse can contribute up to the limit, two qualifying spouses under age 50 have a maximum combined potential contribution of $15,000, which is two times the per-person limit, if joint compensation is at least that much. For a hypothetical couple where both spouses are age 50 or older, that combined total can reach $17,200, which is two times the age-50-and-older limit, if joint compensation is at least that much. Rollover contributions are not subject to the IRA contribution limit, and for 2020 and later there is no age limit on making regular contributions to traditional or Roth IRAs.

Our [couples retirement calculator](/retirement/couples-retirement-calculator/) and [retirement savings calculator](/retirement/retirement-savings-calculator/) are related tools.

sections.heading: Traditional or Roth for the Spouse's Account
sections.body:
Contributions can go to traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs, and the limit applies to the total across both. Review our [Roth IRA vs traditional IRA comparison](/compare/roth-ira-vs-traditional-ira/) to see how the two account structures differ.

If neither spouse participated in a retirement plan at work, all of your contributions to a traditional IRA will be deductible. The deduction may be limited if you or your spouse is covered by a retirement plan at work and your income exceeds certain levels. You can contribute to a traditional or Roth IRA even if you participate in another retirement plan through your employer.

A Roth IRA contribution may be limited based on filing status and income, in addition to the general limit. If you are comparing tax structures for future income, see our guide on [tax-free retirement accounts](/guides/tax-free-retirement-account/) for additional context.

sections.heading: Account Structure and Excess Contributions
sections.body:
A spousal IRA is a contribution rule, not a separate account type. Each spouse can contribute up to the limit, and the combined total is capped by joint taxable compensation.

Contributing more than the allowed amount creates an excess IRA contribution. An excess IRA contribution occurs if you contribute more than the contribution limit, and there is a tax on excess IRA contributions.

sections.heading: Where to Check Your Own Numbers
sections.body:
The IRS pages linked in the sources list the current rules, including the Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA Limit in IRS Publication 590-A. Deduction limits and Roth eligibility depend on income, so confirm the details there.

Tax rules change periodically, and individual household circumstances vary. A CPA or licensed financial professional can advise on your own situation.

faqs.question: Can a non-working spouse have an IRA?
faqs.answer: If you file a joint return, you may be able to contribute to an IRA even if you did not have taxable compensation, as long as your spouse did. Each spouse can contribute up to the current annual limit, provided total combined contributions do not exceed the taxable compensation reported on the joint return.

faqs.question: Can my spouse fund my Roth IRA?
faqs.answer: If you file a joint return, you may be able to contribute to a Roth IRA even if you did not have taxable compensation, as long as your spouse did. Your ability to make a Roth IRA contribution may be limited based on filing status and income, in addition to the general annual contribution limit.

faqs.question: How much can a spouse contribute to a spousal IRA in 2026?
faqs.answer: For 2026, the contribution limit is $7,500, or $8,600 for individuals age 50 or older. If taxable compensation reported on the joint return is less than the annual dollar limit, contributions cannot exceed that compensation amount.

faqs.question: Do we have to file jointly to use a spousal IRA?
faqs.answer: If you file a joint return, you may be able to contribute to an IRA even if you did not have taxable compensation as long as your spouse did. For questions regarding other filing statuses and specific qualification requirements, refer to IRS Publication 590-A.

faqs.question: Is a spousal IRA a joint account?
faqs.answer: A spousal IRA is not a separate account type. It is a contribution rule. Each spouse can contribute up to the limit, capped in total by the taxable compensation on the joint return. Review IRS Publication 590-A for account details.
